mainTopic: The story of יואב's mistaken reading of זכר עמלק, רבא's rule that workers whose mistakes cannot be undone are considered already warned, and רב הונא's ruling about a competing mill in an alleyway.
overview: The amud opens in the middle of a story. דוד המלך asks יואב why he killed only the males of עמלק. יואב says he was taught to read the פסוק as זְכַר ('males') instead of זֵכֶר ('remembrance'). He then confronts his childhood teacher, the two trade פסוקים from ירמיהו, and the story ends with two versions of what happened. רבא then gives a rule: workers whose mistakes cannot be undone, such as a children's teacher, are treated as already warned. A new topic follows. רב הונא rules that a resident of an alleyway may stop a neighbor from opening a competing mill, because it cuts off his livelihood. The גמרא tests this against a ruling about fish traps, the dispute between רבי יהודה and the חכמים about a storekeeper handing out treats, and a ברייתא that allows a shop next to a shop. It concludes that the question is a dispute among תנאים, and that רב הונא follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע then sets out who may block whom: someone from another town, someone who pays the town's tax, and someone from one's own alley. His question about someone from a different alley ends in תיקו. Finally, רב יוסף says that teachers of children may never be blocked, because of עזרא's enactment. The worry that the teachers will grow lazy is answered on the next amud.

steps.title: דוד asks יואב why he killed only the males
steps.stepSummary: דוד asks יואב why he carried out the war against עמלק by killing only the males.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why did you do it this way?
steps.whatsHappening: דוד asks יואב to explain why he killed only the males of עמלק. The question sets up יואב's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מצוה is to wipe out all of עמלק, not only the men. דוד wants to know why יואב did only part of the job.

phrases.english: What is the reason you did this?
phrases.notes: דוד is speaking to יואב, asking why he killed only the males.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a story that began before this section.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why יואב killed only the males of עמלק.

steps.title: יואב cites the פסוק as 'males of עמלק'
steps.stepSummary: יואב answers that the פסוק says to wipe out the 'זְכַר' (males) of עמלק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it is written: 'You shall wipe out the males of עמלק.'
steps.whatsHappening: יואב explains that he followed the פסוק as he understood it, which told him to wipe out the males.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יואב reads the word as זְכַר, meaning 'male'. With that reading, killing only the males seems to be exactly what the פסוק commands.

phrases.english: He said to him: As it is written:
"You shall wipe out the males of Amalek."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers דוד's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק, as יואב read it, said to wipe out the males (זְכַר).

steps.title: דוד: we read it as 'remembrance'
steps.stepSummary: דוד challenges יואב: the accepted reading is זֵכֶר, meaning 'remembrance', which includes everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we read it as 'זֵכֶר' (remembrance)!
steps.whatsHappening: דוד pushes back and says the correct reading of the word is זֵכֶר, not זְכַר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the vowels זֵכֶר, the פסוק means to wipe out the very memory of עמלק, men and women alike. That reading removes יואב's reason for sparing anyone.

phrases.english: He said to him: But we
read it as "zekher" (remembrance)!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges יואב's reading of the פסוק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The accepted reading is זֵכֶר, which includes all of עמלק, so יואב's reason for killing only males falls away.

steps.title: יואב: that is how I was taught
steps.stepSummary: יואב defends himself by saying he was taught to read it as זְכַר.
steps.simpleTranslation: I was taught to read it as 'זְכַר'.
steps.whatsHappening: יואב says the mistake is not his own: this is the reading he was taught as a child.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יואב moves the blame from himself to his teacher. This prepares the next part of the story, where he goes to check with that teacher.

phrases.english: He said to him: I was taught to read "zakhar".

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers דוד's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Places the blame on how he was taught
steps.terutzMaskana: He honestly learned it that way as a child.

steps.title: יואב checks with his childhood teacher
steps.stepSummary: יואב asks his teacher how he taught the word, and the teacher says he read it as זֵכֶר.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went and asked his teacher: 'How did you teach us to read it?' The teacher said: 'זֵכֶר.'
steps.whatsHappening: יואב goes to his old מלמד to find out where the mistake came from. The teacher says he read it correctly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The teacher read the word properly but never noticed that his student was learning it wrong. A small failure in teaching led to a huge mistake in war.
steps.whyThisMatters: This story is why the גמרא stresses careful teaching of children: a mistake learned in childhood stays with a person for life.

phrases.english: He went and asked his teacher,
he said to him: How did you teach us to read?
He said to him: "Zekher".

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on יואב's claim about how he was taught.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The teacher read correctly but did not notice the student's mistake.

steps.title: יואב draws his sword; the teacher asks why
steps.stepSummary: יואב takes a sword to kill the teacher, and the teacher asks why.
steps.simpleTranslation: He took a sword to kill him. The teacher said: 'Why?'
steps.whatsHappening: יואב is furious and moves to kill the teacher. The teacher asks for the reason, which sets up יואב's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The teacher's point is that he did read it correctly, so why should he be punished? יואב will answer with a פסוק.

phrases.english: He took a sword to kill him.
He said to him: Why?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: יואב reacts to learning that the teacher failed him.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the teacher deserves to die.

steps.title: יואב: cursed is one who does God's work carelessly
steps.stepSummary: יואב quotes a פסוק cursing anyone who does God's work carelessly.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it is written: 'Cursed is he who does the work of ה׳ carelessly.'
steps.whatsHappening: יואב justifies himself: teaching תורה is God's work, and the teacher did it carelessly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reading correctly was not enough. The teacher was also supposed to make sure his student learned correctly, and he did not.

phrases.english: He said to him: As it is written:
"Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord with a slack hand."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the teacher's 'why?'.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The teacher did God's work carelessly and is therefore cursed.

steps.title: The teacher: the curse alone is enough
steps.stepSummary: The teacher argues that the פסוק only says he is cursed, so leave him cursed and do not kill him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Leave that man to stay cursed!
steps.whatsHappening: The teacher pushes back: the פסוק gives a curse as the punishment, not death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He accepts that he is cursed but rejects the idea that being cursed means he should be killed. 'That man' is a polite way of saying 'me'.

phrases.english: He said to him: Leave that man
phrases.notes: 'That man' is how the teacher politely refers to himself.

phrases.english: to remain cursed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects יואב's use of the פסוק to justify killing.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the death penalty, not the curse.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The פסוק only speaks of a curse, not of killing.

steps.title: יואב: cursed is one who holds back his sword
steps.stepSummary: יואב answers with the second half of the same פסוק: cursed is the one who holds his sword back from blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written: 'And cursed is he who holds back his sword from blood!'
steps.whatsHappening: יואב answers the teacher with the next words of the same פסוק, which seem to call for using the sword.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the curse applies to יואב himself if he does not strike. So he argues that the curse on the teacher is not the end of the matter.

keyTerms.meaning: Holds back his sword from blood

phrases.english: He said to him: It is written:
"And cursed is he who keeps back his sword from blood"!
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 48:10, the second half of the same פסוק.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the teacher's argument.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings the rest of the same פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The curse is the only punishment.
steps.terutzMaskana: Holding back the sword is itself cursed.

steps.title: Two versions of how the story ended
steps.stepSummary: Some say יואב killed the teacher, and some say he did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say he killed him, and some say he did not kill him.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends without one clear ending: there are two traditions about what יואב did.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Either way, the lesson stands: a mistake learned in childhood can stay with someone for life, so a children's teacher carries great responsibility.
steps.whatToRemember: יואב's war against עמלק went wrong because of a one-vowel mistake learned as a child: זְכַר instead of זֵכֶר. That shows how serious careless teaching is.

phrases.english: There are those who say: He killed him,
and there are those who say: He did not kill him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ending is disputed, but the story shows how dangerous a careless teacher can be.

steps.title: רבא: certain workers are treated as already warned
steps.stepSummary: רבא lists workers who are treated as already warned: a children's teacher, a tree planter, a butcher, a bloodletter, and a town scribe.
steps.simpleTranslation: A children's teacher, a planter, a butcher, a bloodletter, and a town scribe are all considered already warned.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a rule: these workers can be fired for a mistake without first being given a warning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their mistakes cause damage that cannot be fixed. So they are expected to know the stakes from the start, and no warning is needed before letting them go.
steps.confusionAlert: 'מוּתְרִין וְעוֹמְדִין' does not mean these jobs are permitted. It comes from הַתְרָאָה (warning): they are considered warned in advance, so they can be dismissed right away.

phrases.english: And Rava said: A teacher of children,
a tree planter, a butcher, and a bloodletter,
and a town scribe –
all of them are considered as already warned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the story about a careless teacher to a practical rule about teachers and similar workers.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Workers whose mistakes cannot be undone may be dismissed without a prior warning.

steps.title: The general principle: irreversible loss
steps.stepSummary: The rule behind the list: anyone whose mistake causes a loss that cannot be undone is considered already warned.
steps.simpleTranslation: The general rule: any case of a loss that cannot be undone, the worker is considered already warned.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא's list is summed up as one broad rule that explains all the examples.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The common thread is damage that cannot be reversed: a ruined child's learning, a dead tree, a non-kosher animal, harm to a patient's health, a faulty document. The rule can then apply to other jobs like these as well.

keyTerms.meaning: The general principle of the matter
A loss that cannot be undone

steps.whatToRemember: Any worker whose mistake causes damage that cannot be undone is treated as already warned and can be dismissed right away.

phrases.english: The general principle of the matter:
any loss that cannot be undone –
he is considered already warned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: States the principle that ties together רבא's list.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Irreversible loss means the worker is treated as already warned.

steps.title: רב הונא: a neighbor may block a competing mill
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that a resident of an alleyway who set up a mill may stop a neighbor from setting up a competing mill next to his.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a resident of an alleyway set up a mill and another resident came to set up a mill next to him, the first may stop him, because he can say: 'You are cutting off my livelihood.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins: competition between neighbors. רב הונא rules that the first mill owner may block the new one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason is that the second mill would take away the first owner's customers and his income. This opens a discussion about when someone may stop a competitor.

keyTerms.meaning: You are cutting off my livelihood

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the starting point of the classic discussion of הסגת גבול: when one may block a business competitor.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
This resident of an alleyway who set up a mill,
and another resident of the alleyway came
and is setting one up next to him –
the law is that he may prevent him,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the first mill owner, who may stop the newcomer.

phrases.english: as he can say to him:
You are cutting off my livelihood.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא הַאי בַּר מְבוֹאָה דְּאוֹקִי רִיחְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: business competition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An existing mill owner may stop a neighbor in his alleyway from opening a competing mill, because it cuts off his livelihood.

steps.title: A possible support from fish traps
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that a ברייתא about spacing fish traps supports רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say a ברייתא supports רב הונא: A person must keep his fish trap away from the fish of another fisherman, as far as a fish swims.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that might back up רב הונא's ruling against a competing mill. It is setting up a proof that will be examined in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says a new fisherman may not put his trap close to where another fisherman already catches fish. That looks like a rule against crowding someone's established business. This is the same idea רב הונא used for the mill.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say it supports him: the opening words of a suggested proof
One must keep at a distance
How far a fish swims or runs

phrases.english: Let us say this supports him:
phrases.notes: "Him" means רב הונא and his ruling about the competing mill.

phrases.english: One must keep a fish trap away from the fish
phrases.notes: He means the fish that another fisherman is already catching with his trap.

phrases.english: as far as a fish swims.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to support רב הונא's ruling from Step 13.
steps.raayaObject: רב הונא's ruling that one may stop a competing mill in the alleyway.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא requiring distance between fish traps.

steps.title: How far is that distance?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how far the fish trap must be kept away.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how much is that distance?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the actual size of the distance mentioned in the ברייתא. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "As far as a fish swims" is vague, so the גמרא wants an actual measurement. The answer will show how big the protected area is.

keyTerms.meaning: And how much? Asking for an amount or measurement

phrases.english: And how much?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the measurement in the ברייתא from Step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact distance a fish trap must be kept from another fisherman's fish.

steps.title: Up to a פרסה
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא says the distance is up to a פרסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said: up to a פרסה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר רב הונא gives the measurement: up to a פרסה, which is a long distance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פרסה is a large distance. So the ברייתא seems to give strong protection to the first fisherman's area, and that would support רב הונא.

keyTerms.meaning: A פרסה, a long unit of distance (several kilometers)
An אמורא who gives the measurement

phrases.english: רבה בר רב הונא said:
Up to a parasang.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The distance is up to a פרסה.

steps.title: Fish are different
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected: fish are a special case because they scout ahead.
steps.simpleTranslation: Fish are different, because they look around ahead of themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from the fish traps. Fish have a special behavior, so this case does not teach anything about mills.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One fish scouts ahead and the others follow it. Once they meet a trap, they avoid the area, so a new trap close by keeps the fish from ever reaching the first trap. That is a direct blocking of the first fisherman, not just ordinary competition, so no proof for רב הונא comes from here.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different: used to show a case is special

steps.confusionAlert: This does not prove that רב הונא is wrong. It only shows that the fish case is not a proof for him.

phrases.english: Fish are different,
because they look around ahead.
phrases.notes: One fish scouts the path and the rest follow. If they hit the new trap, they turn back and never reach the first one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in Steps 14-16.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof, not רב הונא's ruling.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Fish behave in a special way, so the new trap actually blocks the first one. That is not like an ordinary competing mill.

steps.title: Does רב הונא follow only רבי יהודה?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רבא whether רב הונא's ruling matches רבי יהודה, who forbids a storekeeper from giving treats to children. The חכמים permit it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רבא: Shall we say רב הונא follows רבי יהודה? As we learned in a משנה: רבי יהודה says a storekeeper may not hand out roasted grain and nuts to children, because it gets them used to coming to him. And the חכמים permit it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא suggests that רב הונא's ruling depends on the opinion of רבי יהודה. רבי יהודה forbids a storekeeper from luring customers away from other stores.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רב הונא only follows רבי יהודה, then his ruling goes against the חכמים, who are the majority and allow such competition. That would weaken רב הונא's ruling. The question is really asking whether his view is only a minority opinion.

keyTerms.meaning: He gets them used to coming to him
As we learned in a משנה

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rava:

phrases.aramaic: לֵימָא רַב הוּנָא דְּאָמַר כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה –
phrases.english: Shall we say that Rav Huna ruled like Rabbi Yehuda?
As we learned in a mishna: Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יְחַלֵּק חֶנְוָנִי קְלָיוֹת וֶאֱגוֹזִין לְתִינוֹקוֹת,
phrases.english: A storekeeper may not hand out roasted grain and nuts to children,
because he gets them used to coming to him.
And the Rabbis permit it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא רַב הוּנָא דְּאָמַר כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the fish proof fails, the גמרא asks which תנא רב הונא follows.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רב הונא's ruling depends on the minority view of רבי יהודה against the חכמים.

steps.title: Even the חכמים agree with רב הונא
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים only allow the treats because the other storekeeper can give treats too. Taking away someone's livelihood, like a competing mill, is forbidden even according to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say רב הונא follows the חכמים. The חכמים only disagree with רבי יהודה there, because the storekeeper can say: I hand out walnuts, you hand out almonds. But here, even the חכמים agree, because the first mill owner can say: You are cutting off my livelihood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב הונא fits even with the חכמים. The candy case and the mill case are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the treats, the other storekeeper can fight back fairly by giving treats of his own, so nobody is shut out. With the mill, the new mill takes away the customers the first owner depended on, and he has no equal way to answer. Cutting off a person's livelihood is something even the חכמים forbid.

keyTerms.meaning: You can even say it follows the חכמים
They only disagree up to this point: limiting a dispute

steps.whatToRemember: Ordinary competition, where the other side can respond in the same way, is allowed. Cutting off someone's livelihood is something even the חכמים would forbid, and that is the basis of רב הונא's ruling.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up an important line between fair competition and destroying someone's livelihood. That line is central to the laws of business competition.

phrases.english: You can even say he follows the Rabbis;

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא פְּלִיגִי רַבָּנַן עֲלֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הָתָם –
phrases.english: the Rabbis only disagree with Rabbi Yehuda there
because he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The storekeeper giving out treats is speaking to the other storekeeper.

phrases.english: I hand out walnuts,
you hand out almonds.
But here, even the Rabbis agree,
phrases.notes: "Here" means the case of the competing mill in the alleyway.

phrases.english: because he can say to him:
You are cutting off my livelihood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's question in Step 18.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא's ruling depends on רבי יהודה, and the חכמים would allow the competing mill.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even the חכמים forbid cutting off someone's livelihood. They only allow competition where the other side can answer in the same way.

steps.title: A ברייתא allows a store right next to another store
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says a person may open a shop or bathhouse next to someone else's, and the first owner cannot protest. This seems to contradict רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: A person may build a shop next to his friend's shop, and a bathhouse next to his friend's bathhouse, and the friend cannot protest, because he can say: You work in your own space, and I work in mine!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא with a ברייתא that clearly allows a competing business right next to an existing one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the first owner cannot stop the newcomer, even though the newcomer takes away his customers. That seems to be exactly like the competing mill, which רב הונא said may be stopped. So the ברייתא seems to argue against רב הונא.

keyTerms.meaning: They challenged: introduces a challenge from a תנאי source
To protest against him, to stop him

phrases.english: They challenged:

phrases.aramaic: עוֹשֶׂה אָדָם חֲנוּת בְּצַד חֲנוּתוֹ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ,
phrases.english: A person may set up a shop next to his friend's shop,
and a bathhouse next to his friend's bathhouse;
and the friend cannot protest against him,
because he can say to him:
You work in your own space,
and I work in my own space!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רב הונא against Step 18, the גמרא brings a new challenge against him.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling that one may stop a competing mill in the alleyway.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא allows a competing shop or bathhouse right next to an existing one, because each person works in his own space. That seems to forbid the protest רב הונא allowed.

steps.title: The question is a dispute among תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the contradiction by showing a ברייתא where the תנאים argue. The first opinion says you cannot stop a neighbor from working in the alley. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says you can stop even a neighbor, and רב הונא follows him.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a dispute among תנאים, as a ברייתא teaches: the residents of an alley can force one another not to let a tailor, a tanner, a teacher of children, or any craftsman settle among them. But a person cannot force his neighbor. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: he can force even his neighbor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 20. It says the two sources do not need to agree, because תנאים argue about this very question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא in Step 20, which allows a competing shop, follows the first opinion here: you cannot stop a neighbor. רב הונא's ruling that you can block a competing mill follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who says you can stop even a neighbor. So רב הונא is not contradicted. He simply sides with one תנא.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a dispute among תנאים (the sages of the משנה era)
Residents of an alley or courtyard lane
A tanner, who works with smelly hides
His neighbor, someone who already lives in the alley

steps.confusionAlert: The first opinion is not saying outsiders may come in freely. Everyone agrees that outsiders can be kept out. The argument is only about stopping a neighbor who already lives in the alley.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the classic way the גמרא handles a contradiction from a ברייתא: it shows that the issue is a dispute among תנאים, so an אמורא may side with one of them.

phrases.english: It is a dispute of תנאים,
as it is taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: כּוֹפִין בְּנֵי מְבוֹאוֹת זֶה אֶת זֶה –
phrases.english: The residents of alleys can compel one another
not to settle among them
not a tailor, and not a tanner,
and not a teacher of children,
and not any one of the craftsmen;
but his neighbor he cannot compel.
phrases.notes: This means someone who already lives in the alley. You can't stop him from starting a trade there.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Even his neighbor he can compel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא from the ברייתא in Step 20
steps.terutzResolutionType: Dispute among תנאים: each source follows a different תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא allowing a competing shop seemed to disprove רב הונא outright.
steps.terutzMaskana: That ברייתא follows the first opinion (the רבנן). רב הונא follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who allows blocking even a neighbor.

steps.title: Clear rules: other town, taxpayer, own alley
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע says three things are obvious to him. A resident can block someone from another town. He cannot block an outsider who pays the town's tax. A resident cannot block someone from his own alley.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע said: It is obvious to me that a resident of a town can block a resident of another town. If that person pays tax here, he cannot block him. A resident of an alley cannot block a resident of his own alley.
steps.whatsHappening: A later אמורא gives the practical rules about who can block a competitor and who cannot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An outsider from another town can be kept out. But paying the town's tax makes him count as a local, so he cannot be blocked. Within the same alley, a resident cannot block his neighbor. This follows the רבנן from Step 21, not רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

keyTerms.meaning: He is able to block or prevent

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two levels. Between towns, you can block an outsider. Inside one alley, you cannot block your own neighbor.
steps.whyThisMatters: These rules show how paying the town's tax and belonging to the community decide whether one may protect his business from competition.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ:
phrases.english: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said:
It is obvious to me
a resident of a town, against a resident of another town,
can block him.
And if he shares in the tax of here,
phrases.notes: "Here" means the town where he wants to open his business.

phrases.english: he cannot block him.
A resident of an alley against a resident of his own alley
cannot block him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ: פְּשִׁיטָא לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives practical rulings after the dispute among תנאים in Step 21, siding with the רבנן for one's own alley
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An outsider from another town can be blocked unless he pays the local tax. A resident of one's own alley cannot be blocked.

steps.title: What about someone from a different alley? Unresolved
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע asks whether a resident of one alley can block a resident of a different alley in the same town. The question is left open: תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע asked: A resident of one alley against a resident of another alley, what is the law? Let it stand unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: He asks about the in-between case that his clear rules did not cover, and the גמרא leaves it unanswered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone from another town can be blocked, and someone from your own alley cannot. A person from a different alley in the same town falls between these two cases. It is unclear which side he belongs to, so the question ends with תיקו.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked a question he was unsure about
Let it stand: the question stays unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: Other town: can block. Own alley: cannot block. Different alley in the same town: unresolved (תיקו).

phrases.aramaic: בָּעֵי רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ:
phrases.english: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, asked:

phrases.aramaic: בַּר מְבוֹאָה אַבַּר מְבוֹאָה אַחֲרִינָא, מַאי?
phrases.english: A resident of an alley against a resident of another alley, what is the law?
Let it stand.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the middle case left open by the rules in Step 22
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can a resident of one alley block a resident of a different alley in the same town?

steps.title: Teachers of children can never be blocked
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says that even רב הונא agrees a teacher of children cannot be blocked, because עזרא made a rule to place one teacher next to another.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: רב הונא agrees about teachers of children, that one cannot block them. As the Master said: עזרא made a rule for the Jewish people that they should set up a teacher beside a teacher.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף sets out an exception to רב הונא's rule against competition: teachers of תורה to children.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally רב הונא lets a person block a competitor who would hurt his livelihood. Teaching children is different, because עזרא wanted teachers side by side so the competition would raise the level of teaching. This makes teaching תורה an exception to the usual rule.

keyTerms.meaning: A teacher next to a teacher

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the well-known rule that competition among teachers of תורה is allowed, and even encouraged.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
And Rav Huna agrees regarding teachers of children
that one cannot block them,
as the Master said:
Ezra instituted for the Jewish people
that they should set up a teacher beside a teacher.
phrases.notes: Here סוֹפֵר means a teacher of children, not a scribe.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: וּמוֹדֵי רַב הוּנָא בְּמַקְרֵי דַרְדְּקֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to רב הונא's rule about the mill and adds an exception for teachers
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A teacher of children cannot be blocked from opening next to another teacher, because of עזרא's enactment.

steps.title: Won't the teachers become lazy?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges עזרא's rule: two teachers side by side might rely on each other and become lazy. רב יוסף begins to answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us worry that they will come to be lazy! He said to him:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a worry about placing two teachers together. The final words, אמר ליה, set up רב יוסף's answer, which comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עזרא's rule assumes that competition helps. The challenge argues the opposite: having two teachers might make each one careless, because each can rely on the other. That would defeat the purpose of the rule.

phrases.english: But let us be concerned that they will come to be negligent!
He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב יוסף starting his answer. The answer itself comes right after this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning behind עזרא's enactment cited in Step 24
steps.kashyaTarget: עזרא's enactment to place one teacher beside another
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two teachers together might rely on each other and grow careless, which would undo the benefit of the enactment.
